title: What training does OSHA 1910.269 require for electric power workers?
description: OSHA 1910.269(a)(2) training for power generation, transmission and distribution: qualified employees, annual inspections, retraining, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard 29 CFR 1910.269(a)(2) requires every employee doing electric power generation, transmission or distribution work to be trained in the safety-related work practices for their job, with the degree of training set by risk. Qualified employees need five additional competencies. Employers must check compliance through supervision and at least annual inspections, retrain on defined triggers, and confirm demonstrated proficiency before training counts as complete.
keyTakeaways: Training under 1910.269(a)(2)(i) applies to all employees doing covered work, and its depth is set by the risk of the hazard involved.
A person is not a qualified employee without the five competencies in (a)(2)(ii), including minimum approach distances and determining nominal voltage.
Employers must verify compliance through regular supervision and inspections at least annually under (a)(2)(iv).
Retraining is triggered by non-compliance, new technology, equipment or procedures, or practices not normally used; OSHA treats tasks done less than once a year as needing retraining first.
Training is complete only when the employee has demonstrated proficiency under (a)(2)(viii); the current text does not require a training certification.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Electric utilities and equivalent installations of industrial establishments that operate or maintain generation, transmission and distribution lines and equipment

Qualified and unqualified employees working on or directly associated with covered installations, including fuel and ash handling, water and steam, and chlorine and hydrogen systems at generating stations

blocks.text: Section 1910.269 covers the operation and maintenance of electric power generation, control, transformation, transmission and distribution lines and equipment. Paragraph (a)(1)(i) of [29 CFR 1910.269](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.269) extends it to generation, transmission and distribution installations accessible only to qualified employees; other installations at a generating station, namely fuel and ash handling, water and steam installations that supply energy to generators, and chlorine and hydrogen systems; test sites for electrical testing associated with power generation and delivery; and work on or directly associated with those installations.

The note to (a)(1)(i)(A) confirms that equivalent installations of industrial establishments are covered, while supplementary generating equipment used only for emergency or standby supply falls under Subpart S. Construction work on power lines is governed by 29 CFR part 1926, Subpart V, whose training provision at [29 CFR 1926.950(b)](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.950) opens with the same wording as 1910.269(a)(2)(i)(A).

sections.heading: What training must every covered employee receive?

blocks.text: Every employee doing covered work must be trained in, and familiar with, the safety-related work practices, safety procedures and other requirements of the section that pertain to their job assignments. Paragraph (a)(2)(i)(B) adds any other safety practices related to their work and necessary for their safety, naming emergency procedures "such as pole-top and manhole rescue" as examples. Paragraph (a)(2)(i)(C) states the governing principle: "The degree of training shall be determined by the risk to the employee for the hazard involved."

Under (a)(2)(vi) the training must be of the classroom or on-the-job type. Under (a)(2)(vii) it must establish employee proficiency in the required work practices and introduce the procedures necessary for compliance. Those two clauses together mean that a slide deck alone cannot complete the requirement for hands-on tasks.

sections.heading: What makes someone a qualified employee under 1910.269?

blocks.text: A qualified employee must be trained and competent in five areas listed in paragraph (a)(2)(ii), and the note to that paragraph states that "a person must have the training required by paragraph (a)(2)(ii) of this section to be considered a qualified person." The five areas are:

items: Skills and techniques to distinguish exposed live parts from other parts of electric equipment.
Skills and techniques to determine the nominal voltage of exposed live parts.
The minimum approach distances in the section for the voltages the employee will be exposed to, and the skills and techniques to maintain them.
Proper use of special precautionary techniques, personal protective equipment, insulating and shielding materials, and insulated tools for work on or near exposed energized parts.
Recognition of the electrical hazards the employee may be exposed to, and the skills and techniques to control or avoid them.

blocks.text: Line-clearance tree trimmers who are not qualified employees must be trained and competent in the first three areas under (a)(2)(iii). The glossary entry on [qualified person](/glossary/qualified-person) explains how the term is used across different regulatory regimes.

There is no fixed refresher interval. Instead, (a)(2)(iv) requires the employer to determine, "through regular supervision and through inspections conducted on at least an annual basis", that each employee is complying with the safety-related work practices. The annual element is an inspection of practice, not a classroom session.

Paragraph (a)(2)(v) requires additional training or retraining in three cases: supervision or annual inspections show the employee is not complying; new technology, new types of equipment or changes in procedures require different work practices; or the employee must use safety-related work practices not normally used in their regular duties. The note to (a)(2)(v)(C) adds that OSHA "considers tasks that are performed less often than once per year to necessitate retraining before the performance of the work practices involved."

blocks.title: The infrequent task rule in practice
blocks.text: Rescue, rarely performed switching, and seasonal storm restoration techniques are typical candidates for the less than once a year note. A register of infrequent tasks per role, with a pre-task refresher step, is the practical way to show compliance.

sections.heading: How is completion of 1910.269 training demonstrated?

blocks.text: Completion requires demonstrated proficiency. Paragraph (a)(2)(viii) requires the employer to ensure each employee "has demonstrated proficiency in the work practices involved before that employee is considered as having completed the training." Note 1 says employment records showing successful completion are "one way" to track this, but that they are not required by the paragraph.

Note 2 sets out a three step process for employees with previous training: confirm the employee has the required training; use an examination or interview to make an initial determination that the employee understands the relevant work practices before doing covered work; and supervise the employee closely until proficiency is demonstrated. This is the route for contractors and experienced hires. Older OSHA compilations, such as the 2015 edition of Training Requirements in OSHA Standards (OSHA 2254), reproduce an earlier version of this paragraph that required a certification maintained for the duration of employment, so check guidance against the current eCFR text.

sections.heading: What related training duties sit elsewhere in 1910.269?

blocks.text: Two other paragraphs create training-linked staffing and briefing duties. Under (b)(1), when employees work on or associated with exposed lines or equipment energized at 50 volts or more, persons with first-aid training must be available: at least two trained persons for field work involving two or more employees, and at fixed locations such as substations enough trained persons that each employee exposed to shock can be reached within 4 minutes. Under (c), the employee in charge must conduct a job briefing covering hazards, work procedures, special precautions, energy-source controls and PPE before each job, with at least one briefing before the first job of each day or shift for repetitive work.

blocks.text: Build the curriculum from task analysis and risk, since (a)(2)(i)(C) makes risk the measure of depth. Keep qualified status as a role that is granted only after the five competencies are assessed, and make the annual field inspection the core of the refresher cycle. Utilities that also hold cyber security duties under the North American Electric Reliability Corporation standards can align role mapping with [NERC CIP-004 training requirements](/regulations/nerc-cip-004-training-requirements). See also [how to build a training matrix for an energy utility](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-an-energy-utility), the [energy and resources industry page](/industries/energy-resources), and [OSHA lockout/tagout training](/regulations/osha-lockout-tagout-training-requirements) for hazardous energy control at generating stations. The overview of OSHA duties is at [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats the five qualified employee competencies as separate assessment points and records proficiency against each, so qualified status can be traced to evidence. Infrequent tasks are flagged per role, so the need for retraining before the work is visible when the task is scheduled.

faqs.a: Not as a fixed classroom cycle. Paragraph (a)(2)(iv) requires regular supervision and inspections at least annually to confirm compliance, and (a)(2)(v) requires retraining when those inspections reveal non-compliance or when other triggers apply.

faqs.q: Can an experienced lineworker from another utility start work immediately?
faqs.a: Note 2 to (a)(2)(viii) allows an employer to confirm the prior training, use an exam or interview to make an initial determination of understanding before covered work begins, and then supervise closely until proficiency is demonstrated. Training is not complete until proficiency is shown.

faqs.q: Is a training certificate required under 1910.269?
faqs.a: The current text does not require one. Note 1 to (a)(2)(viii) says employment records showing successful completion are one way to track proficiency. Some older guidance reproduces an earlier certification requirement, so rely on the current eCFR text.

faqs.q: Does 1910.269 apply to power line construction?
faqs.a: Construction of transmission and distribution lines and equipment is covered by part 1926, Subpart V. Its training provision, 1926.950(b), uses the same opening language as 1910.269(a)(2), so curricula are often shared across both.

factCheck.claim: 1910.269(a)(1)(i)(A)-(D) scope: generation, transmission, distribution installations; fuel and ash, water and steam, chlorine and hydrogen systems at generating stations; test sites; note on industrial establishments and Subpart S standby equipment.
1910.269(a)(2)(i)(A)-(C): training in safety-related work practices; other practices incl. pole-top and manhole rescue; degree of training determined by risk.
1910.269(a)(2)(ii)(A)-(E) five qualified employee competencies; note: must have this training to be a qualified person; (a)(2)(iii) line-clearance tree trimmers first three.
1910.269(a)(2)(iv) regular supervision and inspections at least annually; (a)(2)(v)(A)-(C) retraining triggers; note: tasks less than once per year need retraining before performance.

1910.269(a)(2)(vi)-(viii): classroom or on-the-job; establish proficiency; demonstrated proficiency before completion; Note 1 records one way, not required; Note 2 three step process for previously trained employees.

1910.269(b)(1): first-aid trained persons at 50 volts or more; two trained persons for field work with two or more employees; fixed locations reach within 4 minutes; (c) job briefing subjects and at least one before first job of each day or shift.
1926.950(b)(1)(i): each employee trained in and familiar with safety-related work practices pertaining to job assignments (Subpart V).
OSHA 2254 (2015) reproduces earlier 1910.269(a)(2)(vii) certification maintained for duration of employment.
